study.title: Amos 7 - intercession, measure of God and confrontation with prophetic rejection
study.overview: Amos 7 presents a sequence of visions and a direct confrontation between the word of God and the religious and political resistance in Israel. In the first two visions, severe judgments are announced, but the prophet intercedes and the Lord suspends destruction. In the third vision, however, the image of the plumb appears: God is measuring his people with righteousness and proclaiming that he will not continue to cheer him. The second half of the chapter shows the reaction of Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, who tries to silence the prophet, and the answer of Amos, who claims not to speak for his own career, but by divine calling. The chapter ends with a hard sentence on Amaziah, showing that rejecting the messenger of God does not neutralize the word of God, but aggravates guilt.

outline.title: Two views of judgment suspended by intercession
outline.explanation: God shows Amos a devastation for locusts and then a judgment by fire. In both cases, the prophet pleads mercy to Jacob, recognizing the littleness and fragility of the people, and the Lord revokes the judgment at that time.

outline.title: The plumb and the rupture between the prophetic word and religious power
outline.explanation: In the third vision, the Lord places a plumbing in the midst of Israel, a sign of a straight assessment and condemnation. The sanctuary and the high idolatry will be destroyed. Amaziah reacts by accusing Amos of conspiracy and attempts to expel him from Bethel, because the message threatens the religious center and the throne.

outline.title: The authority of the call and the sentence on Amaziah
outline.explanation: Amos denies being a prophet by profession or inheritance; he states that he was taken by God's work in the field to prophesy in Israel. Therefore, the silence imposed by Amaziah is confronted with a new word of the Lord, which announces shame, loss of the family, division of the earth and exile into an unclean land.

study.context: The chapter mentions Bethel as a place of sanctuary and the royal palace, indicating the connection between worship and power in resistance to Amos. Amaziah appears as Bethel priest and loyal to King Jeroboam; he treats prophecy as a political threat, not as the word of God. The notes also highlight that the locusts were a real threat to livelihood, especially when they attacked late planting, and that the image of the plumb communicates strict justice standard. Moreover, the text shows a national crisis: the accusation of Amaziah presupposes that the message of Amos includes the death of Jeroboam and the captivity of Israel.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter unites mercy and judgment without contradiction. In the first verses, God hears intercession and suspends deserved punishments, revealing patience; but this patience is not infinite. The vision of the plumbology teaches that God not only threatens, but evaluates his people according to a just standard and does not tolerate indefinitely infidelity. The chapter also affirms God's sovereign freedom in calling who he wants: Amos is not legitimized by religious origin, institutional formation or support of the palace, but by sending the Lord. Finally, opposition to Amos shows that rejecting the prophetic word is an act of rebellion against God himself, and that the attempt to preserve political or religious stability can become complicity with idolatry and injustice.

scholarViews.insight: The note highlights that Amaziah acted to keep the king satisfied and preserve his office, showing allegiance to the throne more than to God's word.
The comment notes that when the conflict is between God and man, it is easy to predict who will come out in worse condition; Amos' denunciation against Amaziah culminates in court over the accuser.
The image of the plumb is understood as a symbol of strict justice, indicating that God would measure Israel according to its iniquity.

questions: When God postpones a judgment, does this lead me to repentance or presumptuous confidence that nothing will happen?
In which areas do I prefer to hear messages that reassure me instead of the straight word of God that corrects me?
Have I recognized the call and authority of the word of God even when it confronts my interests, my reputation or my loyalties?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to unite prayer and submission. The practical application is to examine whether there are areas in which spiritual life seems outwardly correct, but has already been placed under the plumbing of God. He also urges not to hostile biblical correction for personal interest, as Amaziah did. In the life of the church and the family, it is worth cultivating humility to receive warning, readiness to intercede for others and courage to obey God above human approval. When the Word confronts, the wise answer is to repent, adjust life to God's standard and not try to silence the truth.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the sequence of visions, the role of Amaziah and the general sense of the plumb and exile. However, they do not detail all external historical elements or confirm later unfolding of each individual threat. Therefore, no data were added on dates, archaeology, authorship of the book or identification of original terms beyond what the notes already explain.
